results.answer:
Take word = 'Python' and prefix = 'Py'. word[-1] is the last character: 'n'. word[2:5] slices from position 2 included to 5 excluded: 'tho'. word[42] raises IndexError: string index out of range because the word only has 6 characters. word[42:] is an out-of-range slice and is handled gracefully: it returns ''. Strings are immutable, so word[0] = 'J' raises TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment. To change the first character to J, create a new string, e.g. 'J' + word[1:] -> 'Jython'. prefix 'thon' fails because you cannot concatenate a variable and a string literal; it raises SyntaxError: invalid syntax. The correct way is to use +: prefix + 'thon' -> 'Python'. When printing a Windows path C:\some
ame, 'C:\some
ame' lets 
 mean newline, so print(r'C:\some
ame') preserves the backslashes and prints C:\some
ame. Raw strings have the limitation that a raw string may not end in an odd number of \ characters; see the FAQ entry for more information and workarounds.
results.excerpt:
>>> word[-1]  # last character
'n'

>>> word[2:5]  # characters from position 2 (included) to 5 (excluded)
'tho'

>>> word[42]  # the word only has 6 characters
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
IndexError: string index out of range

>>> word[42:]
''

>>> word[0] = 'J'
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment

If you need a different string, you should create a new one:

>>> 'J' + word[1:]
'Jython'

>>> prefix = 'Py'
>>> prefix 'thon'  # can't concatenate a variable and a string literal
  File "<stdin>", line 1
    prefix 'thon'
           ^^^^^^
SyntaxError: invalid syntax

If you want to concatenate variables or a variable and a literal, use +:

>>> prefix + 'thon'
'Python'

>>> print('C:\some\name')  # here \n means newline!
C:\some
ame
>>> print(r'C:\some\name')  # note the r before the quote
C:\some\name

There is one subtle aspect to raw strings: a raw string may not end in
an odd number of \ characters; see
the FAQ entry for more information
and workarounds.
